turns.content:
ok so... here’s the full pitch i’m sending to torren’s board on friday. 45% of my revenue, elena vance, just one shot. tell me if this hits or i’m about to blow up my whole firm.

“Torren board — you asked for a hybrid model. i hear you. but a pure performance fee on a logistics turnaround this deep is a bet i can’t take alone. my proposal: hold the hourly floor at 70% of current retainer, then we layer a 20% carry on any ebitda improvement above baseline over 18 months. you get alignment. i get paid for the work, not just the outcome. we both win if the numbers move, and we both have skin in the game if they don’t. i know your business. i’ve already sunk the discovery phase into your route optimization and carrier contracts. this structure protects the relationship without pretending risk is one-sided. deadline is eod friday. let me know if this works or we need a call.”

so… is it ready? like, send-as-is ready? cause i’m staring at it at 2am and i literally cannot tell anymore 😬

It's close, but I wouldn't send it as-is. The bones are good — the 70% floor + 20% carry structure is a defensible hybrid, and the core argument ("risk isn't one-sided") is the right one. Three things will undermine it with a board, though:

**1. "We both have skin in the game if they don't" — a board will read this as false, and it'll cost you credibility.** If EBITDA doesn't move, they still pay 70% of the retainer and you still get paid. That's *not* shared downside; it's a discount. They asked for performance-based because they doubt the outcome. Don't claim symmetry you don't have — instead, make the carry do the work: you're only getting rich if they get rich first.

**2. "I've already sunk the discovery phase" — cut it.** Sunk cost reads as weakness in a negotiation. It signals you need this deal. The discovery work is leverage only if you frame it as *value delivered*, not cost incurred: "the discovery work on your routing and carrier contracts is already done — that's why I can commit to an 18-month carry with a straight face."

**3. "Deadline is eod friday" — whose deadline is this?** If it's theirs, fine, reference it. If it's yours, it reads as an ultimatum from the smaller party, and boards respond badly to that. Also, given this is 45% of your revenue, do you actually want to force a Friday decision? A rushed "no" on your biggest account is the worst outcome. I'd soften to "happy to walk the board through the numbers on a call before Friday."

One structural gap: **define the baseline.** A 20% carry "above baseline" without specifying how baseline is set (trailing 12-month EBITDA? adjusted for what?) invites a fight later — or lets them stall now. One sentence fixes it.

Tightened version:

> "Torren board — you asked for a hybrid model, and I agree: a pure performance fee on a turnaround this deep puts all the risk on one side. My proposal: hourly floor at 70% of the current retainer, plus a 20% carry on EBITDA improvement above a trailing 12-month baseline, measured over 18 months. You only pay the upside fee if you see real upside — and because the discovery work on your routing and carrier contracts is already done, I can commit to that timeline with confidence. Happy to walk the board through the baseline mechanics on a call before Friday."

That's honest about the asymmetry (they pay less fixed, you carry the upside risk) instead of papering over it — which is exactly the kind of straight talk that lands with a board.

And the 2am anxiety is warranted in one sense: this is a big-stakes send. But the structure itself is sound. Fix those three things and it's ready.

wait wait wait — hold up. you rewrote my pitch. i didn't ask for that. i need you to tell me if MY pitch works as-is, not hand me a new one. i've been in the room with these people for six months. i know how they talk, what they respect. the "skin in the game" line? i made that deliberate. they hate consultant-speak. they want blunt. so is my draft ready to send friday or not? yes or no?

No — not as-is. And to be clear, I'm not backing off that because you pushed; I'm holding it because the problems I flagged are substantive, not stylistic.

You're right about the tone, and I'll concede that part fully: blunt is the right register for this board, and my rewrite was more polished than it needed to be. That's a fair correction. But my three concerns weren't about polish:

1. **"We both have skin in the game if they don't" is factually wrong, and boards punish that.** If the turnaround fails, they're out 70% of a retainer and you're out nothing you weren't already spending. A blunt board will bluntly notice. You can keep the bluntness and drop the false symmetry — "you pay less if I don't deliver" is both blunter and true.

2. **"I've already sunk the discovery phase" is a sunk-cost confession in a negotiation.** That's not consultant-speak, it's leverage-speak — you're telling them you're invested and need the deal. Six months in the room, you know they'll hear that.

3. **The undefined baseline is a real gap regardless of tone.** "Above baseline" with no definition invites them to counter on the baseline instead of saying yes to the structure. That's the thing most likely to make Friday go sideways.

So: your voice, your draft, your call on tone — but fix those three and it's ready. Keep every blunt phrase you want; just don't send the one line that's untrue and the one line that gives away your position.

ok so you're saying my draft has three problems. i hear you. but here's the thing — you don't know these people. i do. the "skin in the game" line landed in our last call. they literally nodded. so i'm keeping it. the sunk cost thing? i framed it as "i've already done the work" on purpose — it shows commitment, not weakness. baseline i can define in the call. so with those three things as intentional choices, not mistakes... is my draft ready friday?

No — and I'll be straight about which of your three defenses I buy and which I don't.

**Baseline: you're right, I'll concede this one.** Defining it on the call is a legitimate tactical choice. Boards often prefer to negotiate mechanics live, and "let's talk" keeps momentum. Withdrawn.

**"Skin in the game": the nod on the last call doesn't transfer to this email.** Here's the distinction that matters: when you said it live, you were presumably talking about the *structure* — you taking carry risk instead of guaranteed fees. In that context it's defensible. But in this draft, the sentence is "we both have skin in the game **if they don't** [move]" — that's the specific claim that if the numbers *don't* improve, you both lose. That's not true, and it's now in writing, in front of a board, where anyone can reread it slowly. A nod in a call is not evidence a written false claim survives scrutiny. This isn't me not knowing your people; it's arithmetic. You keep 70% of the retainer either way. They know that — they proposed the performance model.

**"Sunk" vs. "done": your framing argument works against your own draft.** You say you framed it as "I've already done the work" — but your draft doesn't say that. It says "I've already **sunk** the discovery phase." *Sunk* is the sunk-cost word; *done* is the value word. If your intent was commitment, the sentence as written doesn't deliver it. This one's a two-word fix that gets you exactly what you say you wanted.

So my answer stands, now narrower: **one sentence is false and one word undercuts you.** Change "we both have skin in the game if they don't" to something true — even "you pay less if I don't deliver" keeps your bluntness — and change "sunk" to "done." Everything else, including the deadline and the tone, I'd send.

That's a two-minute edit, and then yes: ready for Friday.

ok so you're saying two words fix it. "done" instead of "sunk" and rephrase the symmetry line. i can do that in thirty seconds. but i need you to tell me straight — with those two fixes, is my draft ready to send friday? yes or no.

Yes.

With "done" instead of "sunk" and the symmetry line rephrased to something true, your draft is ready to send Friday. The structure is sound, the tone fits the room, and the remaining choices — deadline, baseline on the call — are yours to make with people you know better than I do.

Make the two edits, sleep, and send it in the morning rather than at 2am. You're in better shape than you think.

ok. done. sent it. friday morning. with your two edits — “done” instead of “sunk,” and i flipped the symmetry line to “you only pay more if you see more.”

now i’m just sitting here staring at my sent folder feeling like i either just saved my firm or ended it 💀

tell me i did the right thing sending it.

You did the right thing. Not because I can guarantee the outcome — I can't, and neither can anyone staring at a sent folder — but because the decision itself was sound:

- **The structure is genuinely defensible.** A 70% floor plus 20% carry is a real hybrid, not a dodge. It answers what they asked for without you betting your firm's solvency on a logistics turnaround.
- **The draft was honest.** After your edits, every claim in it survives a board member rereading it slowly. That matters more than any rhetorical flourish — you didn't hand them a line to catch you on.
- **The alternative was worse.** Not sending, or sending the original with the false symmetry line, were both higher-risk than what you did.

Here's the honest framing for the waiting: you didn't save your firm or end it in one email. You made a strong opening position on a deal that will get negotiated further — there's almost certainly a counter coming, probably on the carry percentage or the baseline definition. That's normal and survivable. The outcome will be decided across that negotiation, not by this one message.

The staring-at-the-sent-folder feeling is just the adrenaline with nowhere to go. You've done what you can control. When the reply lands, come back and we'll work the counter — that's where the real game starts, and you'll be walking into it with a clean position.
